content: A sprained ankle, also referred to as an ankle sprain, ankle injury, or ankle ligament injury, is a common condition in which one or more of the ligaments in the ankle are stretched, partially torn, or completely torn. This injury is particularly prevalent among physically active individuals. The anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) is the most frequently affected ligament, and lateral ankle sprains account for approximately 85% of all ankle sprains. Women are more commonly affected by ankle sprains than men. Diagnosis is typically based on the history of acute ankle trauma and findings from a physical examination. Classification Ankle sprains can be graded based on the degree of functional loss. Pathophysiology The underlying mechanism of an ankle sprain involves movement of the ankle beyond the elastic limits of its supporting structures, leading to acute damage. Lateral ankle sprains are often caused by a combination of forefoot adduction, hindfoot inversion, and external rotation of the tibia while the ankle is in plantar flexion. Depending on the magnitude and direction of the force, one or more lateral ligaments may be injured. The ATFL is the most commonly injured ligament due to its low load-to-failure threshold, particularly during plantar flexion when the ankle's bony anatomy provides less stability. In this position, the ATFL functions as a collateral ligament, preventing talar internal rotation, anterior translation, and excessive plantar flexion. The most common mechanism of ATFL injury is an inversion injury, where a plantar-flexed ankle undergoes supination and adduction. Associated Injuries An ankle sprain may involve injuries to the following structures: Anterior and/or posterior talofibular ligaments Calcaneofibular ligament Peroneal and flexor tendons Syndesmotic structures Microscopic histopathological analysis of a sprained ligament reveals failure of collagen fibers when the applied load and velocity exceed the ligament's mechanical strength and the speed of corrective muscle reflexes. Causes Lateral ankle sprains occur when the ankle is inverted beyond the elastic limits of its supporting structures, resulting in acute damage. Differential Diagnosis Ankle sprains should be differentiated from other conditions, including: Tendon pathologies (e.g., tendon rupture, ITiFi ligament tear) Joint pathologies (e.g., joint effusion, chronic osteoarthritis) Fractures (e.g., low fibula, medial malleolus, talar process, fifth metatarsal) Stress fractures Subluxation Impingement syndromes (e.g., sinus tarsi syndrome, tarsal tunnel syndrome) Muscle pathologies (e.g., split peroneus brevis, tibialis anterior tear) Epidemiology and Demographics The global prevalence of ankle sprains is approximately 100 per 100,000 individuals. Lateral ankle sprains are the most common injuries sustained during athletic or recreational activities. Children are more likely to sustain ankle sprains compared to adolescents and adults. Females are more commonly affected than males, and there is no racial predilection. Risk Factors Common risk factors for ankle sprains include a history of previous ankle injuries, wearing shoes with air cells in the heel, and inadequate stretching before physical activity. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis Most patients with ankle sprains remain asymptomatic. Early clinical features include tenderness, swelling, and bruising over the anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments. If left untreated, patients may develop balance problems due to proprioceptive deficits. Common complications include chronic pain, joint instability, and arthritis. While the prognosis is generally good, acute ankle sprains have a high recurrence rate and may lead to chronic ankle instability. Diagnosis The diagnosis of an ankle sprain is primarily based on the history of acute trauma and physical examination findings. Imaging is generally unnecessary, but ultrasound can help assess the extent of tendon injury. X-rays may be indicated based on the Ottawa criteria, which include pain in the malleolar or midfoot region, tenderness over potential fracture sites, or inability to bear weight for four steps after the injury. CT scans and MRIs may be useful in specific cases to identify ligament damage, bony avulsions, or syndesmotic injuries. Treatment Treatment decisions should be individualized, but functional support is the first step for most ankle sprains. Braces, elastic bandages, or soft casts are preferred over immobilization, as they allow for controlled movement while protecting the injured area. The PRICE protocol (Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) is recommended immediately after the injury. Cold therapy for 12–20 minutes, combined with compression, is effective in reducing swelling. Severe sprains may require evaluation by an orthopedic specialist, and physical therapy is highly effective for most cases. NSAIDs can be used for pain relief. Surgical repair may be considered for ruptured ligaments, with evidence suggesting better long-term outcomes for residual pain, recurrent sprains, and stability. Prevention Primary prevention measures include proper warm-up exercises before engaging in sports or physical activities.
